281: A is correct because enabling a Multi-AZ deployment for the RDS instance provisions a standby instance in a separate Availability Zone with synchronous replication, which delivers an RPO of effectively near zero, well under 1 second, and automatic failover if the primary fails. Read replicas and DMS CDC replicate asynchronously, so they cannot guarantee a sub-second RPO, and single-AZ auto scaling does not provide replication at all.
282: B is correct because security groups support referencing another security group as a traffic source, so configuring the EC2 instances' security group to allow inbound traffic only from the ALB's security group restricts access exclusively to the load balancer and blocks all other sources inside or outside the private subnet. This is the intended pattern for private-subnet targets behind an ALB, whereas the other options either do not restrict access or bypass the ALB entirely.
283: D is correct because Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP is a single managed file system that can present the same data over both NFS and SMB protocols simultaneously, so the Linux simulation application and the Windows visualization application can share one synchronized data set without code changes. This eliminates the data duplication and double infrastructure of maintaining two separate file systems, meeting the requirement to migrate both applications unchanged.
284: B is correct because Cost Explorer natively provides cost and usage reports that can be grouped by dimensions such as linked account and IAM user, and the report can be scheduled and downloaded as CSV for building department budgets. This is the most efficient built-in approach, requiring no pipeline setup or SQL queries, while the billing dashboard, Athena, and Budgets do not directly deliver a per-user billed items report.
285: B is correct because an Amazon API Gateway endpoint backed by AWS Lambda calling Amazon SES is a fully serverless solution with zero idle cost, which is ideal for fewer than 100 visits per month since you only pay per request. It provides the dynamic server-side processing the contact form requires, and it is far more cost-effective than always-on options like EC2, ECS, or Lightsail that charge continuously regardless of traffic.
286: C is correct because the deployments to Amazon S3 are succeeding, but CloudFront continues serving previously cached copies of the objects from edge locations until their TTL expires, which is why the website does not show updates. Creating a cache invalidation for the updated objects forces CloudFront to fetch the new versions from the S3 origin, making the changes visible, whereas load balancers, caching layers, or certificates would not address stale edge cache content.
287: B is correct because hosting all three tiers on Amazon EC2 instances preserves full access to SQL Server features like native backups and Data Quality Services, which are not fully supported on Amazon RDS. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed native SMB shared storage that the Windows-based application and business tiers can consume for inter-tier file processing. EFS and EBS are not appropriate here because the workload requires Windows-native SMB file sharing accessible by multiple instances.
288: C is correct because Amazon EFS is a managed NFS shared file system that can be mounted concurrently on all the Linux web servers, giving each instance access to the same shared content without any application changes. EBS volumes can only be attached to a single instance at a time, and S3 or CloudFront would require rewriting the application to change how it accesses files.
289: B is correct because attaching an IAM execution role to the Lambda function with a least-privilege IAM policy granting read access to that specific S3 bucket follows AWS best practice of granting only the required permissions via temporary credentials. Embedding long-term access keys in code is insecure, a bucket policy alone is less precise for this scenario, and granting read access to all buckets in the account violates least privilege.
290: C is correct because a mix of On-Demand and Spot Instances lets the Auto Scaling group use cheaper Spot capacity for interruptible demand while relying on On-Demand Instances as a reliable baseline, optimizing cost without any long-term commitment. Reserved and Dedicated Instances both require commitments that the company wants to avoid, and On-Demand alone would not maximize savings.
291: A is correct because signed cookies control access to CloudFront content without changing the URLs themselves, which serves the users who cannot modify their hardcoded URLs since authorization is delivered via the cookie rather than the link. B is correct because signed URLs control access through the URL itself, which works for users with custom HTTP clients that do not support cookies. Using both methods together covers both user groups with the least impact, while AppSync, JWTs, and Secrets Manager do not provide CloudFront content access control.
292: A is correct because Kinesis Data Streams ingests the real-time streaming data, Kinesis Data Analytics transforms it with SQL or Flink processing, Kinesis Data Firehose delivers it to Amazon S3, and Athena provides on-demand SQL queries over the transformed data in S3, fully meeting every requirement. B is correct because Amazon MSK streams the data, AWS Glue can run the transformation and write results to Amazon S3, and Athena then queries that transformed data with standard SQL. The other options fail because DMS is for database migration rather than streaming ingestion, and the RDS query editor cannot query data stored in S3.
293: D is correct because a stored volume gateway keeps the complete primary dataset on local on-premises storage while asynchronously and securely backing it up to Amazon S3 over TLS, preserving local access to all the data and providing an ongoing managed backup process. A cached volume gateway only keeps frequently accessed data locally, and Snowball devices are one-time migration tools rather than a continuous backup solution.
294: B is correct because a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 enables private connectivity between the EC2 instances and the S3 bucket using the VPC's private address space and route tables, so traffic never traverses the internet or requires public IP addresses. NAT gateways still route traffic over the internet, and Route 53 hosted zones or VPN connections do not provide private access to S3.
295: B is correct because S3 Object Lambda automatically intercepts and transforms data at the point of retrieval, so the PII can be stripped for the two applications that must not process it while the third application receives the full data, all from a single stored copy. This avoids the operational overhead of maintaining separate transformed datasets in multiple buckets or tables or building and operating a custom proxy layer.
296: D is correct because VPC peering requires non-overlapping CIDR blocks between the two VPCs, and the development VPC already uses 192.168.0.0/24, so any 192.168.x range is invalid. A VPC must be at least a /28 in size, which rules out the /32 options, leaving 10.0.1.0/24 as the smallest valid non-overlapping CIDR block that supports the peering connection.
297: B is correct because a target tracking scaling policy based on the ASGAverageCPUUtilization metric automatically adds and removes instances to hold average CPU at the 50% target, ensuring capacity during the 65% surges while reducing the overprovisioned fleet (min 2, max 6, desired 3) to optimize cost. The other options either require manual intervention, risk availability by terminating instances below load, or add operational burden instead of automation.
298: C is correct because a subnet exists within exactly one Availability Zone, so provisioning one subnet in each AZ allows the Auto Scaling group to spread EC2 instances across both zones for redundancy. Configuring the RDS DB instance for Multi-AZ deployment creates a synchronous standby in the second zone with automatic failover, making the application highly available. Options with subnets spanning multiple AZs are invalid because subnets cannot extend across Availability Zones, and a DB instance with only network connections lacks database-level failover.
299: B is correct because FSx for Lustre with persistent SSD storage is a high-performance parallel file system designed for exactly this workload, delivering sub-millisecond latencies and hundreds of GBps of aggregate throughput across hundreds of Linux EC2 instances, and its S3 integration lets data be imported from the raw S3 bucket and exported back after processing. Persistent HDD storage provides higher latencies that fail the sub-millisecond requirement, and FSx for NetApp ONTAP does not scale to the same aggregate throughput levels for this distributed processing pattern.
300: C is correct because the application runs 24/7 with steady, predictable utilization, making EC2 Reserved Instances far cheaper than On-Demand for the application tier. Amazon Aurora automatically grows database storage as needed, eliminating capacity management, and reserving the Aurora instances locks in a significant discount for the always-on database tier. Spot Instances are unsuitable for a continuously running critical workload, and On-Demand pricing would waste money for steady-state usage.
